idiom_name: goroutine fan-out + sync.WaitGroup join (errgroup when a failure must cancel siblings)
implementation_notes: Fork/join is absorbed into the language: the go statement starts each branch and a sync.WaitGroup, errgroup.Group or a channel-based join collects them, so the classic task pool and its worker objects simply disappear into the recursive function. Keep the cut-off - goroutine creation plus scheduler traffic costs more than a short leaf loop - and bound wide fan-outs with a semaphore channel or a fixed worker pool instead of one goroutine per subproblem. Results must travel through per-branch variables or channels and be combined in the parent: a shared accumulator is a race the race detector will find.
code_sketch:
func MergeSort(a []int) []int {
    if len(a) < 1024 { return insertionSort(a) }       // base case
    mid := len(a) / 2
    var left, right []int
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    wg.Add(2)
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); left = MergeSort(a[:mid]) }()
    go func() { defer wg.Done(); right = MergeSort(a[mid:]) }()
    wg.Wait()
    return merge(left, right)                          // combine
}
pitfalls: Each branch needs its own destination variable: two goroutines writing the same slice element is a data race even though the join appears to order them.
Unbounded goroutine fan-out per level queues huge numbers of goroutines and defeats the scheduler's balancing - bound depth or width.
A plain WaitGroup does not cancel siblings when one branch fails; use errgroup.Group (or a context) when partial results must not survive a failure.
